lesson_title: The Bucket Under a Hot Sky: South Africa's Water in Four Facts
hook_text: Of every 100 litres of rain that fall on South Africa, only 9 ever reach a river.
clip_script: Picture South Africa's whole water supply as one bucket in the yard, filled only by rain. Fact one: the tap runs weak. We get about 465 millimetres of rain a year. The world average is 860. We start at barely half. Fact two: the sun works against the bucket all day. Over most of the country, the sky can evaporate MORE water in a year than it drops — in parts of the Northern Cape, five times more. Every dam and puddle is quietly steaming back into the sky. Fact three: the tap splashes. Of every 100 litres that fall, only about 9 ever reach a river where we can catch them. The rest evaporates, feeds plants, or sinks away. Fact four: the tap is not over everyone. The east coast gets over 1 000 millimetres; drive west and it dies away to less than 50 — one good storm per YEAR. That is why our rivers give up as they go west, from always flowing, to summer only, to dry beds that roar once in a decade. And it is why we built more than 500 big dams and named a crisis Day Zero. A weak tap, a thirsty sun, a 9 per cent catch, and the rain falling far from the people. Now you understand every water debate in this country.
visual_style: A single bucket under a blazing animated sun; rainfall bars shrinking west across a South Africa map; 100 falling droplets with only 9 landing in a river; a dam counter climbing past 500.
pacing: Four rapid facts each with a visual punch, a westward drive-time montage, one-line summary landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for the rivers, dams and aquifers behind the numbers.
